newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean telecoms face mixed Q3 fortunes - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Chilean telecoms face mixed Q3 fortunes - analysts.

text.p: Chilean telecoms will show a mixed bag of gains and losses when they report third quarter earnings starting Friday, with Compania de Telecomunicaciones de Chile expected to make a strong showing, analysts said.

Chile's telecommunications industry, one of the world's most advanced, has moved past last year's bruising competition in long-distance rates to face now a complex future of mergers, alliances and acquisitions.
"Prices have bounced back to where people are making money," said William Beavington of Paribas Capital Markets.

Paribas estimates CTC will report earnings per American Depositary Receipt of $1.75, versus $1.52 in the same quarter of 1995. CTC is expected to report its earnings Friday and other telecoms will follow suit next week.

"I don't see any new price wars," said Paula del Sol of Santander Investment. "Companies are now more convinced of the value of being comfortable with their prices and are concentrating more on marketing the name and the image, and not so much the price."

Santander sees CTC earnings per ADR at $1.59, Telex-Chile at $0.04 per ADR compared to $0.06 in the same quarter of 1995 and Entel at 11.4 Chilean pesos per share from six pesos in third quarter 1995.
A Salomon Brothers report forecast CTC earnings at $1.65 per ADR in the third quarter, and Merrill Lynch saw CTC at $1.76.
"CTC is probably the best-managed phone company in Latin America, and it has the second best line growth in Latin America," said Ray Ligouri of Merrill Lynch.

Entel, Telex-Chile and a few smaller outfits are starting to pinch pieces off CTC's core business -- local telephone service. But over 90 percent of local phone service in Chile is still CTC, and analysts see only a slight and very long-term threat to CTC's business in that area.
"It's just the other side of the competitive coin," said Beavington. "Telex and Entel have been talking for years about getting into local service and I don't see much has come of it."

For now, only CTC offers local service in the whole country. Del Sol said efforts by CTC's competitors to move into that area were probably part of the tide toward complete telecom packages -- local service, long-distance, mobile phones, Internet and cable TV all wrapped up and offered to consumers at one price.

It's known as one-stop telecom shopping. And Chile, as in most telecom advances, is getting into the act faster than the United States and may prove to be a kind of testing ground, as it was for the popular multicarrier long-distance system.
Entel, CTC and VTR, owned 40 percent by SBC Communications Inc, are already well-advanced in developing telecom packages "but I think all companies are moving in that direction," said del Sol.

"That's exactly what's going on in the United States and what Telmex is planning for Mexico," said Beavington, adding that the advantage for consumers is that they receive one bill for a vast variety of services.
"Chile is arguably the most competitive telecoms market in the world, and it's ahead of the United States" in developing telecom package services, he added.

As the rush to offer package services increases, companies are more likely to start merging in a few select areas, analysts said. CTC and VTR pointed the way earlier this year when they merged their mobile phone divisions to create Startel.

Telex-Chile and BellSouth Chile, a unit of BellSouth, have long been reported to be looking into some kind of alliance, and long-distance carrier Entel was recently in talks with local phone firm Telefonica Manquehue.
